cases.title: Joël Le Scouarnec — surgeon convicted for 299 victims
cases.who: Joël Le Scouarnec (surgeon); hospitals and medical regulators
cases.what: Le Scouarnec, a surgeon in western France, was convicted in Saintes in December 2020 of raping and sexually assaulting four children, including two of his nieces (15 years). At his second trial in Vannes he admitted abusing all 299 victims, mostly hospital patients, many under anaesthesia or waking from surgery, between 1989 and 2014; more than 250 were under 15. On 28 May 2025 the court sentenced him to the maximum 20 years. He is not part of an elite network; included as a professional whose standing protected him (setting is debatable — could be moved to 'care').
cases.cover_up: The FBI traced his downloading of abuse images in 2004; his 2005 conviction (4 months suspended) brought no restriction on practice. Prosecutors did not alert medical authorities; the regional medical body found no breach in 2006; a 2007 warning to the health ministry brought no action; a hospital hired him in 2008 knowing of the conviction.

cases.title: Chad — Zoé's Ark tries to fly 103 children to France (convicted 2007)
cases.who: French charity L'Arche de Zoé (founder Éric Breteau)
cases.what: In October 2007 members of the French charity Zoé's Ark were detained in Chad as they tried to fly 103 children to France; the charity said they were orphans from Sudan's Darfur region, but authorities found most were from Chad and not orphans. On 26 December 2007 a Chadian court convicted six French members of attempting to kidnap the children and sentenced them to eight years' forced labour, and ordered each to pay €60,000 to each of the 103 children; a Chadian and a Sudanese defendant got four years and two Chadians were acquitted. The six were transferred to France, and Chad's President Idriss Déby pardoned them at the end of March 2008.

cases.title: Freedom Hosting — Tor host for Lolita City and other abuse sites
cases.who: Freedom Hosting (Eric Eoin Marques, convicted)
cases.what: Freedom Hosting was a free anonymous dark web hosting service that ran from July 2008 to July 2013 and hosted over 200 child exploitation websites, including Lolita City, which Anonymous had attacked in 2011. The operator, Eric Eoin Marques, was arrested in Dublin in early August 2013 on a US warrant; the FBI accused him of being 'the largest facilitator of child porn on the planet'. After Ireland's Supreme Court dismissed his challenge in March 2019 he was extradited, pleaded guilty on 6 February 2020 to conspiracy to advertise child sexual abuse material, and on 16 September 2021 was sentenced to 27 years. DOJ said the sites held millions of images and videos, over 1.97 million not previously known to law enforcement.
cases.cover_up: Extradition from Ireland took from 2013 to 2019 through appeals.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

cases.title: Hugh Nelson — first UK prosecution for AI-made abuse images
cases.who: Individual offender selling commissioned AI-transformed images
cases.what: Nelson, 27, used 3D software with an AI function to turn ordinary photos of real children, some supplied by people who knew them, into abuse imagery, selling it in chatrooms for about £5,000 over 18 months. Greater Manchester Police caught him after he told an undercover officer he charged £80 per 'character'. Convicted of 16 offences including encouraging the rape of a child under 13, he was sentenced at Bolton Crown Court on 28 October 2024 to 18 years. Police identified suspects and victims in Italy, France and the US.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Regpay — Minsk-based paid abuse sites / Operation Falcon
cases.who: Regpay Co. Ltd (Belarus) with Florida payment firm Connections
cases.what: Regpay Co. Ltd of Minsk, Belarus, processed paid memberships to about 50 websites, including child abuse sites it operated itself, serving thousands of subscribers worldwide; payments were laundered with help from Connections USA of Fort Lauderdale, Florida. US Attorney General John Ashcroft announced the case in January 2004 as part of Operation Falcon. Regpay's president Yahor Zalatarou and marketing director Alexei Buchnev were arrested at a Paris hotel on 30 July 2003 after a ruse by US agents, and technical administrator Aliaksandr Boika was arrested in Tarragona, Spain, on 31 July 2003 and extradited. All pleaded guilty in New Jersey. Buchnev was sentenced to 40 months in May 2006; Zalatarou and Boika were each sentenced to 25 years on 9 August 2006. Connections' chief executive pleaded guilty to money laundering. Hundreds of subscribers were arrested in the US and other countries.

cases.title: Bernard Preynat and Cardinal Barbarin, Lyon
cases.who: Archdiocese of Lyon; Fr Bernard Preynat; Cardinal Philippe Barbarin
cases.what: Fr Bernard Preynat was accused of abusing about 80 Boy Scouts between 1971 and 1991; many cases were time-barred and he was tried for assaults on 10 minors from 1986 to 1991. A church tribunal found him guilty and removed him from the priesthood (announced 4 July 2019), and on 16 March 2020 a Lyon court sentenced him to five years in prison. Cardinal Philippe Barbarin was convicted in March 2019 of not reporting him and given a six-month suspended sentence; an appeal court acquitted him in January 2020 and the Cour de cassation upheld that in April 2021. Pope Francis accepted his resignation on 6 March 2020.
cases.cover_up: Cardinal Barbarin convicted in March 2019 of failing to report abuse (suspended six months), cleared on appeal and by France's highest court in April 2021

cases.title: CIASE (Sauvé Commission) — Catholic Church in France
cases.who: Catholic Church in France (commissioned by bishops and religious orders)
cases.what: The Independent Commission on Sexual Abuse in the Church, chaired by Jean-Marc Sauvé, reported on 5 October 2021. Using a population survey, it estimated about 216,000 people were abused as minors by clergy and religious from 1950 to 2020, and about 330,000 including lay people working in church institutions. Archive research put the number of abusive clergy and religious at 2,900 to 3,200, a floor of 2.5% to 2.8% of the roughly 115,000 who served, and it described the abuse as massive and its causes as systemic.
cases.cover_up: Commission called the abuse 'massive' and 'systemic' and said the church must accept institutional responsibility

cases.title: France — CIIVISE final report on sexual violence against children (2023)
cases.who: French justice, health and child-protection systems; families and institutions
cases.what: The Independent Commission on Incest and Sexual Violence against Children (CIIVISE), created by the government on 11 March 2021 and chaired by juvenile judge Édouard Durand, delivered its final report on 20 November 2023 with 82 recommendations. It estimated that 160,000 children suffer sexual violence each year in France. It found that victims wait 10 to 13 years on average for specialised care and that only 5% of reports come from doctors. The commission's work covers abuse in families and in institutions, and the failures of courts, police and health services to act.

cases.title: France — children in state child welfare (ASE) exploited in prostitution
cases.who: Aide sociale à l'enfance (departmental child welfare services)
cases.what: A French parliamentary commission of inquiry report published in April 2025 estimated that about 15,000 children in the care of the departmental child welfare services (ASE), which hold about 396,900 minors, are victims of prostitution. Lawyers asked the Bouches-du-Rhône and Essonne departments for administrative reviews over children in care who were prostituted; teenagers are often housed in hotels with little supervision. A complaint was filed with the UN Committee on the Rights of the Child.

cases.title: El Salvador — children disappeared by the armed forces during the civil war (Pro-Búsqueda)
cases.who: Salvadoran armed forces
cases.what: Pro-Búsqueda, founded in 1994, has documented close to a thousand children disappeared during the Salvadoran civil war, mostly by the armed forces; many were adopted through flawed procedures to the US, France, Spain, Italy and the Netherlands. On 1 March 2005 the Inter-American Court of Human Rights ruled on the 1982 disappearance of the Serrano Cruz sisters during the 'Guinda de Mayo' military operation. El Salvador created a National Search Commission for Disappeared Children in 2010.
cases.cover_up: The armed forces have not granted access to archives on disappeared children despite years of lobbying.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: Notre-Dame de Bétharram school — National Assembly commission of inquiry
cases.who: Notre-Dame de Bétharram, a Catholic private school under contract with the state; Ministry of Education inspection
cases.what: Priests, teachers and staff are accused of sexual and physical abuse of pupils from 1957 to 2004, with about 200 complaints filed in 2025. The National Assembly commission of inquiry (rapporteurs Violette Spillebout and Paul Vannier) published its report on 2 July 2025 with 50 recommendations, including rebuilding state inspections. It did not directly implicate François Bayrou, who said he had not grasped the seriousness of information he received; Vannier separately accused him of misleading parliament.
cases.cover_up: The commission wrote that 'in the absence of action from a minister who was informed and in a position to intervene', abuse continued for years; it found state inspection of private schools under contract was weak and sanctioned teachers could move between schools undetected.

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Fr Johannes Rivoire — Oblate in Nunavut, never extradited from France
cases.who: Oblates of Mary Immaculate (OMI Lacombe Canada; Oblates of France)
cases.what: French Oblate Johannes Rivoire worked in the Canadian North from 1959 to 1993. He faced at least three sexual-abuse charges (1998 warrant) concerning Inuit children in Arviat, Rankin Inlet and Naujaat, and a 2022 warrant for indecent assault on a girl in Arviat and Whale Cove between 1974 and 1979. A March 2024 review by retired Quebec justice André Denis, commissioned by the Oblates, concluded on the preponderance of evidence that he assaulted six children. Inuit Tapiriit Kanatami called his death without trial in April 2024 'a systemic failure of nation states and religious institutions'.
cases.cover_up: He left for France in January 1993; a Canadian arrest warrant followed in 1998 and charges were later stayed. A 2022 warrant led to an extradition request that French authorities denied. The 2024 Denis review found the RCMP never contacted the Oblates when charges were laid. In February 2024 the Vatican ruled against his dismissal. He died in France in 2024 without trial.

flows.title: Seoul → France
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to France; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Bucharest → France
flows.what: Romanian intercountry adoptions to France in 2002, during the moratorium period before the 2004 ban.

flows.title: Abéché → France (removal)
flows.what: Zoé's Ark attempted to fly 103 children to French host families; six members convicted in Chad.

flows.title: France → CAR: Sangaris soldiers accused (offenders)
flows.what: Allegations of child sexual abuse; French judges dismissed the case for insufficient charges.

flows.title: Paris → United States (Brunel / MC2 modelling)
flows.what: French prosecutors investigated rape of minors and trafficking linked to Epstein and model agent Jean-Luc Brunel, whose MC2 agency in New York and Miami was reportedly funded by Epstein. Brunel was charged but died before trial, so no court finding exists.

flows.title: Gabriel Matzneff: France → Philippines
flows.what: Matzneff made several trips to the Philippines in the 1980s and described sex tourism with underage boys in his published diaries; there was no prosecution.

flows.title: Abuse material hosted in France (IWF 2025)
flows.what: France's share rose from 1% (2024) to 7% in 2025.

flows.title: France → Madagascar (tourist offenders)
flows.what: Foreign tourists, often from France, exploit Malagasy children.

flows.title: Nunavut → France: Fr Johannes Rivoire
flows.what: Rivoire left the Arctic for France in January 1993; Canadian warrants (1998, 2022) went unexecuted and France refused extradition. He died in France in 2024.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: L'Arche de Zoé (Zoé's Ark)
networks.what: French charity whose six members were convicted in Chad in December 2007 for trying to fly 103 children, falsely presented as Darfur orphans, to French host families.

networks.name: UN peacekeeping operations (Department of Peace Operations)
networks.what: UN Secretary-General reports record 357 SEA allegations against peacekeeping personnel in 2006, falling to 51 in 2014 and rising to 102 in 2024. In 2024, 27 of 125 identified victims were children. Most allegations since 2018 come from MONUSCO (DRC) and MINUSCA (CAR). Criminal accountability rests with troop-contributing countries; the UN can only repatriate.

networks.name: Operation Sangaris (French army, CAR)
networks.what: French military operation in the Central African Republic, December 2013 – October 2016. Allegations of child sexual abuse by its soldiers in Bangui (2013–2014) ended in a judicial dismissal (non-lieu) in January 2018.

networks.name: Jeffrey Epstein and associates
networks.what: Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.

networks.name: Freedom Hosting
networks.what: Largest Tor web host in 2013, hosting Lolita City and other abuse sites; operator sentenced in the US to 27 years (2021).

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boylover forum
networks.what: 'Discussion-only' forum used to make contact before sharing abuse material privately; 670 suspects, 184 arrests, 230 children safeguarded (Operation Rescue, 2011).

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2007: OIOS investigation of MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent (2007).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: States that shielded their own
patterns.role_note: Sri Lankan peacekeepers in Haiti (MINUSTAH): None convicted by Sri Lanka; one-off ex gratia payment to one victim (2016)
patterns.pattern_summary: When a person accused of abusing a child is a soldier, a diplomat or a foreign citizen, whether they are tried depends on their own government. UN peacekeepers can be prosecuted only by the country that sent them. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had sexually exploited and abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007; 114 were sent home, and none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In 2013 the Vatican recalled its ambassador to the Dominican Republic, Archbishop Józef Wesołowski, while Dominican authorities were investigating him for abusing children, and later told Polish prosecutors that Vatican law did not allow him to be extradited. In 2020 a court in Seoul refused a US request to extradite Son Jong-woo, who had run the abuse website Welcome to Video. In 2013 Morocco's king pardoned Daniel Galván, a Spanish man convicted of raping children, as a gesture towards Spain. In Israel, a deputy health minister interfered with psychiatric assessments of Malka Leifer, which delayed her extradition to Australia for several years.

patterns.pattern: The adoption pipeline that keeps moving
patterns.role: Sending country, later closed or suspended
patterns.role_note: 13,986 children sent abroad 2003–2022 (Selman). 2007: scandal: centre forced to return 47 children held for international adoption (IOM) 2010: scandal: 10 US missionaries arrested taking 33 children to the Dominican Republic (29 January); about 1,090 children brought to US under humanitarian parole
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Peacekeepers and aid workers in crisis zones
patterns.role: Mission or crisis zone where children were abused
patterns.role_note: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti. Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued.
patterns.pattern_summary: In war zones and refugee camps, children have been sexually abused by soldiers and aid workers sent to protect them or to provide food and shelter. In 2002 a report by the UN refugee agency and Save the Children described aid workers and peacekeepers in Guinea, Liberia and Sierra Leone trading food and other aid for sex with children. In Haiti, a UN investigation found that Sri Lankan peacekeepers had abused at least nine children between 2004 and 2007, and 114 soldiers were sent home; none was jailed in Sri Lanka. In the Central African Republic, children reported abuse by French soldiers and UN troops in 2014 and 2015; French judges closed the case against the French soldiers in 2018 without charges. An independent commission found 83 alleged perpetrators among people working on the World Health Organization's Ebola response in the Democratic Republic of the Congo between 2018 and 2020, 21 of them WHO staff, and victims as young as 13. The UN has published yearly counts of these allegations against peacekeepers since 2004.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children
patterns.role: Abductions and sexual violence by armed groups
patterns.role_note: Haiti — armed gangs' sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024).
patterns.pattern_summary: Armed groups have abducted, enslaved and sold children as a deliberate practice. In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Where children are abused for paying viewers
patterns.role_note: US and Canadian faith-based donors → Haitian orphanages.
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti; Haiti — restavek child domestic servitude and gang exploitation of children (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Haiti — New Life Children's Refuge: US missionaries try to take 33 children after earthquake
cases.who: New Life Children's Refuge (Idaho Baptist missionaries) led by Laura Silsby
cases.what: On 29 January 2010, after the earthquake, ten American Baptist missionaries were detained trying to take 33 Haitian children to the Dominican Republic without proper documentation; their interpreters said group members had spoken with the children's parents. They were charged on 4 February 2010 with kidnapping and criminal association. In February a judge released eight, concluding they had not knowingly committed a crime, and later a ninth; the kidnapping and criminal association charges were dropped. On 17 May 2010 the organiser, Laura Silsby, was convicted of arranging illegal travel under a 1980 law restricting movement out of Haiti and sentenced to the 3 months and 8 days she had already served.

cases.title: Haiti — orphanage assessment identifies 3,019 potential trafficking victims
cases.who: Private orphanages in Haiti; Institut du Bien-Être Social et de Recherches (IBESR)
cases.what: The US State Department's 2019 Trafficking in Persons Report states that Haiti's social welfare agency IBESR, 'after completing an assessment of more than 750 orphanages with another government and international NGOs, identified 3,019 potential victims of trafficking in those institutions'. IBESR closed eight non-compliant orphanages in the reporting period and expanded foster care to 121 accredited families to reduce children's vulnerability to trafficking.

cases.title: Haiti — armed gangs' sexual violence against children (UN verified 2024)
cases.who: Viv Ansanm gang coalition (411 cases) and other armed gangs
cases.what: The UN verified sexual violence against 566 children (523 girls, 43 boys) in Haiti in 2024, 411 attributed to the Viv Ansanm coalition; cases involved rape (406) and gang rape (160). This was up from 41 girls verified in 2023. Viv Ansanm was listed in the Secretary-General's annex for rape and other sexual violence against children, recruitment, killing and maiming, and attacks on schools and hospitals.

cases.title: MINUSTAH Sri Lankan contingent — child sexual exploitation ring, Haiti
cases.who: Sri Lanka Army contingent of the UN Stabilization Mission in Haiti (MINUSTAH)
cases.what: In November 2007, 114 members of the 950-strong Sri Lankan contingent were accused of sexual misconduct and abuse, and 108, including three officers, were sent home. The UN Office of Internal Oversight Services concluded that 'acts of sexual exploitation and abuse (against children) were frequent and occurred usually at night, and at virtually every location where the contingent personnel were deployed', and said charges should include statutory rape. An Associated Press investigation in April 2017 found that at least 134 Sri Lankan peacekeepers had exploited at least nine children in a sex ring between 2004 and 2007; none was jailed.
cases.cover_up: Repatriation instead of prosecution: 114 Sri Lankan peacekeepers were sent home; Sri Lankan authorities judged the acts 'consensual' and nobody was jailed.

cases.title: Oxfam GB in Haiti — 2011 investigation; possible involvement of minors not pursued
cases.who: Oxfam GB staff in the 2010 earthquake response, including the country director
cases.what: Oxfam GB's 2011 internal investigation found staff in Haiti had used prostitutes, some of whom were alleged to be 'underage'. The Charity Commission's June 2019 inquiry found that not all lines of enquiry about minors were pursued and that Oxfam did not adequately investigate allegations in an email of 18 July 2011 that minors were being sexually abused by Oxfam employees, nor report them to the Commission or law enforcement. The Commission said it was no longer possible to conclude with certainty whether minors were involved or at risk.
cases.cover_up: Staff including the Belgian country director were allowed to resign; Oxfam did not report the allegations of abuse of minors to the Charity Commission or police in 2011.

cases.title: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice
cases.who: Flemish adoption services; intermediaries in Ethiopia and other countries of origin
cases.what: After reports of malpractice in adoptions from Ethiopia in 2019, the Flemish government appointed an independent expert panel on intercountry adoption, which delivered its findings in 2021 (final report dated 15 February 2023), and funded the Flemish Centre for Adoption to examine Ethiopian adoptions from 1997 to 2015. Preliminary conclusions found that the true story sometimes differed from the adoption files and that in the worst cases children had not been given up voluntarily by their birth parents. The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

cases.title: UN — Zeid report: 45% of 2004 peacekeeping SEA allegations involved sex with under-18s (2005)
cases.who: UN peacekeeping military and civilian personnel
cases.what: On 24 March 2005 the Secretary-General transmitted the report of his adviser Prince Zeid Ra'ad Zeid Al-Hussein on sexual exploitation and abuse in UN peacekeeping. Of 105 allegations recorded across missions in 2004, about 45% involved sex with persons under 18; in MONUC (DR Congo) 72 allegations were received between May and September 2004, and women interviewed described 'rape disguised as prostitution', with sex often costing about $1 to $3. OIOS considered 7 of the MONUC cases it examined fully substantiated and found convincing evidence in 2 more. The report recommended binding standards for all personnel, a professional investigative capacity, on-site courts martial and DNA paternity testing.

cases.title: Haiti — 2007: children trafficked for international adoption returned to parents
cases.who: A Haitian centre holding children awaiting international adoption
cases.what: In 2007 a Haitian centre was forced to return 47 children awaiting international adoption to their families, after misleading parents with payments and holding the children in 'inhumane conditions' for months or years, according to the International Organization for Migration. An October 2007 report said officials had returned 50 trafficked children with 100 more awaiting rescue.

cases.title: Lumos — 'Funding Haitian Orphanages at the Cost of Children's Rights'
cases.who: Mostly privately run, foreign-funded orphanages in Haiti; donors 92% from the US and 90% faith-based
cases.what: Lumos researched Haiti's orphanages from October 2016 to February 2017, including a 2016 evaluation of 140 children in four orphanages with the government agency IBESR, and published its report in June 2017. It found at least US$70 million a year going to about a third of orphanages, with total funding estimated above $100 million a year; only 15% of orphanages were registered and at least 140 had conditions putting children at severe risk. It documented violence and severe neglect and, in a few cases, sexual abuse, trafficking and avoidable deaths, and evidence of orphanages recruiting children away from families — an 'orphanage business' it describes as increasingly recognised as trafficking.

cases.title: Haiti — restavek child domestic servitude and gang exploitation of children (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Host families (restavek); armed gangs
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says a large share of Haiti's trafficking cases involve children in restavek domestic servitude, often physically abused and unpaid, and that displacement from Port-au-Prince increased children's risk of sexual exploitation in the restavek system. Gangs exploit women and girls in sex trafficking; an international organization reported close to 50 per cent of gang members are children, with a 70 per cent rise in child recruitment in 2024.
cases.cover_up: Observers report police and immigration officials complicit at the Haiti–Dominican Republic border.

cases.title: Haitian Football Federation — Yves Jean-Bart banned by FIFA
cases.who: Yves Jean-Bart (FHF president since 2000)
cases.what: On 30 April 2020 The Guardian reported accusations that Jean-Bart, president of the Haitian Football Federation since 2000, coerced young female players at the national training centre in Croix-des-Bouquets into sex; he denies the allegations. On 18 Nov 2020 FIFA's Ethics Committee banned him from football for life. On 14 Feb 2023 the Court of Arbitration for Sport annulled the ban; FIFA appealed to the Swiss Federal Tribunal in March 2023 (outcome not checked). patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2016: UN COI on Syria — 'They came to destroy': ISIS crimes against the Yazidis (2016).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: War and the taking of children

In 2014 the group calling itself Islamic State captured Yazidi women and children in northern Iraq and sold girls as sexual slaves; a UN commission reported in 2016 that more than 3,200 women and children were still held. In 2014 Boko Haram abducted 276 schoolgirls from Chibok in north-eastern Nigeria, and 82 were still captive in 2024. The Lord's Resistance Army abducted children in Uganda and the neighbouring countries over many years; in 2021 the International Criminal Court convicted one of its commanders, Dominic Ongwen, on 61 counts, including forced marriage and sexual slavery. UN fact-finding missions found sexual violence against children by Myanmar's army and by Sudan's Rapid Support Forces, against girls as young as eight. The UN verifies and publishes these attacks country by country each year.

patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. patterns.role_note: 2001: moratorium: United States suspends adoptions from Cambodia (late 2001) 2004: conviction: Lauryn Galindo pleads guilty in US to visa fraud and money-laundering conspiracy over Cambodian adoptions
patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. In each of these, investigations found children who had been bought, taken from their families or falsely registered as orphans, and adoptions were stopped or suspended by the sending country, the receiving countries, or both. In 2025 South Korea's Truth and Reconciliation Commission found the state responsible for human rights violations in its overseas adoptions. Receiving countries also began to investigate: the Netherlands suspended all intercountry adoption in 2021 after a government committee reported abuses, and China ended the practice in 2024. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Travelling offenders: crack down here, it moves there
patterns.role_note: 1996: Cambodia: 1996 Law on Suppression of the Kidnapping, Trafficking and Exploitation of Human Persons 2002: Svay Pak (Phnom Penh): child prostitution "bustling", driven by Western child-sex tourism after child prostitution in Thailand was cracked down upon 2003: 22 January 2003 police raid on Svay Pak child brothels — widely advertised in advance; no arrests; nearly all children moved beforehand to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. A Dateline NBC–IJM operation later in 2003 rescued 37 girls 2005: Cambodian government shut down Svay Pak brothels (2005); by 2006 prostitutes "no longer operate[d] with impunity"; 2008 Dateline: brothels "moved out of town"; 2011 CNN: trade had gone underground 2008: Cambodia: Law on Suppression of Human Trafficking and Sexual Exploitation (2008)
patterns.pattern_summary: The records show offenders who travel abroad to abuse children moving to new places as old ones were policed. In the Philippines, the mayor of Manila closed the Ermita district in 1992, and many of its bars reopened in Angeles City, where the US Clark Air Base had closed the same year. Observers reported that child prostitution in Svay Pak, on the edge of Phnom Penh in Cambodia, grew after Thailand cracked down in the 1990s, and that when police raided Svay Pak in January 2003 the raid had been announced in advance and most of the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville. The countries the offenders came from passed laws allowing their citizens to be prosecuted for abusing children abroad: Germany in 1993, Australia in 1994, Canada in 1997, Japan in 1999 and the United States in 2003. Later the abuse moved online. In the Philippine cities where the charity International Justice Mission worked with police, the number of children sold in bars and on the street fell by 79 to 86 percent between 2006 and 2016. Between 2014 and 2017, the number of Philippine internet addresses used each month for the sexual exploitation of children rose more than twelvefold.

cases.title: Cambodia — Lauryn Galindo adoption-fraud conspiracy; US moratorium 2001
cases.who: US facilitator Lauryn Galindo and associates; Cambodian officials paid by facilitators
cases.what: The US imposed a moratorium on Cambodian adoptions in late 2001 after fraudulent cases and raids by the Cambodian rights group LICADHO. In 2004 she pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering in 17 cases, admitting she falsified documents that erased children's identities (she denied trafficking), and faced an 18-month sentence. Some adoptive families later found their children had living relatives.

cases.title: Gary Glitter (Paul Gadd) — UK, Cambodia and Vietnam cases
cases.who: Paul Gadd ('Gary Glitter', pop singer)
cases.what: Convicted in the UK in 1999 of possessing thousands of child abuse images (about 4,000; jailed four months). He was expelled from Cambodia in 2002 amid sex-crime allegations. In March 2006 a Vietnamese court convicted him of obscene acts with two girls aged 10 and 11; he spent about two and a half years in jail there. In February 2015, after Operation Yewtree, he was convicted of attempted rape, four indecent assaults and one count of sex with a girl under 13, against three girls in 1975–1980, and sentenced to 16 years. cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)

cases.title: UNTAC Cambodia — growth of prostitution around peacekeepers
cases.who: UN Transitional Authority in Cambodia (UNTAC) personnel (about 15,900 military)
cases.what: The arrival of UNTAC's roughly 22,000 personnel was followed by a sharp rise in prostitution, from an estimated 6,000 to more than 25,000 sex workers in two years, and by abuse of Cambodian women and girls; the UN did not keep thorough records of allegations at the time, so numbers rest on later academic reconstruction. cases.title: Svay Pak child brothels — 2003 raid and later decline
cases.who: Brothels in Svay Pak (mostly ethnic Vietnamese victims)
cases.what: Svay Pak, a poor fishing village on the outskirts of Phnom Penh, became notorious as a place where foreign men bought sex with children; CNN in 2017 reported girls there being sold by their families. cases.cover_up: The 22 January 2003 police raid was widely advertised in advance; almost all children had been moved and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had extorted brothel owners.

cases.who: Brothel and entertainment operators; foreign and Cambodian offenders
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Cambodian men and men from Australia, South Africa, the United States and other countries in Asia and Europe sexually exploit children in the tourism industry, increasingly via social media; children as young as 13 are exploited in brothels to pay family debts; and women and girls are exploited in online scam compounds.

cases.title: Morocco — royal pardon of Spanish child rapist Daniel Galván (2013)
cases.who: Daniel Galván Viña
cases.what: Daniel Galván Viña, a retired Spanish professor, was arrested in Morocco in December 2010 and in September 2011 sentenced to 30 years for raping 11 Moroccan children aged 4 to 14. In late July 2013 he was among 48 Spanish prisoners pardoned by King Mohammed VI; after protests outside parliament in Rabat, the king revoked the pardon on 4 August 2013, citing the gravity of the crimes and the victims' rights, and said he had not been told the details of the case. Galván had already left Morocco; he was later arrested in Spain.

cases.title: Belgium (Flanders) — expert panel and Ethiopia investigation on intercountry adoption malpractice

The panel's report led to screening of every country of origin, after which Flanders stopped adoptions from Vietnam and then from Gambia, Haiti and Morocco.

patterns.pattern_summary: Intercountry adoption is the adoption of a child from one country by parents in another. From the 1950s onward the children came from a series of countries in turn. South Korea sent about 164,000 children abroad between 1953 and 2008. Later the main sources included Romania in the 1990s, Guatemala until 2008, Cambodia, Vietnam, Nepal and Ethiopia. The map draws 59 documented adoption flows and marks which sending countries were later closed or suspended.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

patterns.pattern: Where nobody is counting
patterns.role: No survey data on online abuse in its region
patterns.role_note: Childlight's 2026 update found South Asia lacking representative survey data on technology-facilitated child sexual exploitation.
patterns.pattern_summary: Most counts of child abuse and trafficking come from three sources, and each leaves large parts of the world out. The first is surveys that ask a representative sample of people about their experiences. Childlight, a research centre that combines such surveys into global estimates, had them from only 60 countries in its 2026 update, too few to represent South Asia, West and Central Africa, or the Middle East and North Africa. The second is official statistics that governments send to the UN; its 2024 global report on trafficking covered 156 countries, but only 72 supplied figures for 2023. The third is reports from technology companies to the US CyberTipline; in 2025, 14 percent of its 23.4 million reports could not be assigned to any country, and North Korea had 12, a number that reflects how few people there can use American apps. The research for this map also found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in Italy, Brazil, the Philippines or India.

cases.title: Nepal — National Human Rights Commission national reports on trafficking: an estimated 5,000 children trafficked in a year
cases.who: Trafficking networks moving women and girls across the open border to India and on to third countries
cases.what: Nepal's National Human Rights Commission, through its Office of the Special Rapporteur on Trafficking in Persons, has published national reports on trafficking since 2005. Its report released in August 2019 estimated that about 35,000 Nepalis were trafficked in 2018, including 5,000 children, and that nearly 1.5 million were at risk. It said nearly 1,000 Nepali women and girls are rescued from India each year and that poor screening at the open border makes cross-border trafficking hard to control. Its 2018 report said girls and women are trafficked to India for prostitution, orchestra dancing, circus work and marriage, and some are moved on to third countries.

cases.title: 'Hidden in Plain Sight' — Australian Parliament recognises orphanage trafficking as modern slavery
cases.who: Australian volunteers, donors, schools and tour operators supporting overseas orphanages
cases.what: The Joint Standing Committee's report 'Hidden in Plain Sight', released on 6 December 2017 from its inquiry into establishing a Modern Slavery Act, recognised orphanage trafficking as a form of modern slavery to be covered by the Act. A chapter was devoted to orphanage trafficking, orphanage tourism and Australian donations, with evidence from ReThink Orphanages, Lumos, the ChildSafe campaign and others. Australia's Modern Slavery Act followed in 2018; Lumos supported the change.

cases.title: SOS Children's Villages — Independent Special Commission (ISC) worldwide report (2023)
cases.who: SOS Children's Villages (federation of member associations; International Senate); former senior staff
cases.what: An Independent Special Commission appointed by the International Senate of SOS Children's Villages in 2021, chaired by former Kenyan Chief Justice Willy Mutunga with former Delhi High Court acting chief justice Gita Mittal, issued its summary report on 6 June 2023. Using a 'reasonable grounds to believe' standard, it confirmed serious allegations of child sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found cover-ups of past sexual abuse and failures to report to national authorities in more than one association. Countries named in the report include Nepal, Cambodia, India, Kenya, Panama, Sierra Leone and Syria. A confidential 991-page part two went to the organisation's Senate and Executive Board on 2 May 2023; in November 2025 SOS Children's Villages International said it was examining whether parts could be passed to prosecutors.
cases.cover_up: Former senior staff in some member associations knew of abuse and failed to act or concealed reports; serious abuse was not reported to national authorities.

cases.title: Nepal — Hague Conference mission finds regular falsification of papers to make children 'adoptable' (2010)
cases.who: Child-care homes and intermediaries in Nepal's intercountry adoption system; foreign adoption agencies
cases.what: At the request of Nepal's Ministry of Women, Children and Social Welfare, the Permanent Bureau of the Hague Conference on Private International Law sent a technical assistance mission to Nepal on 23–27 November 2009; its report is dated 4 February 2010. It cited evidence that documents were regularly falsified to declare children adoptable, with false statements about abandonment, origin, age and status, and that this continued under the 2008 rules. It said the USD 5,000 per-child payment and USD 10,000 annual agency fee created strong incentives unrelated to the cost of care, and that Nepal had no data on adoptable children.

cases.title: Kolkata red-light areas — rescues of trafficked Nepali girls and minors (2015, 2025)
cases.who: Brothel keepers and traffickers in Kolkata
cases.what: In January 2015 police, with International Justice Mission and three NGOs, freed six young women trafficked from Nepal from four brothels in Kolkata's largest red-light area; all had fake adult ID documents, which IJM said traffickers issue to underage girls. On 10 September 2025 Kolkata Police's Anti-Human Trafficking Unit rescued ten people including nine minor girls from a house in Burtolla, North Kolkata, and arrested six people, including the couple running it (charged). The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers recruit significant numbers of Nepali and Bangladeshi women and girls for sex trafficking in India.

cases.title: Nepal child care homes — 'paper orphans' and recruitment by agents
cases.who: Child care homes (orphanages) in Nepal, many registered as NGOs; recruiting agents
cases.what: Nepal's National Child Rights Council counted 417 registered child care homes holding 10,905 children in 2021/22, and UNICEF estimates about 85% have a living parent or guardian. Agents take money from rural families with promises of schooling and are paid commissions by institutions; NGOs documented a child admitted on a forged parental death certificate. Researchers say homes use children to attract donations and that many operate unregistered. Only about 200 of 753 local governments had appointed the child welfare officers required by the Act Relating to Children (2018).

cases.title: Nepal — baby-buying in intercountry adoption; 2007 shutdown
cases.who: Orphanages and adoption intermediaries
cases.what: A Daily Telegraph investigation in March 2007 described baby-buying, bribes and deception of birth families. In April 2007 Nepal's new minister halted all intercountry adoptions, leaving about 400 Western families waiting; about 440 pending cases were processed after November 2007, and new rules were published in May 2008. UNICEF and Terre des hommes published 'Adopting: The Rights of the Child' in August 2008. Wikipedia records that the US later suspended adoptions of children declared abandoned because documents were unreliable.

cases.title: Nepal → India — trafficking of girls to Indian brothels (estimates)
cases.who: Trafficking networks recruiting via false job, marriage and online romance offers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers use job offers and online romance scams to recruit Nepali women and children to India for sex trafficking; Nepali courts convicted 406 traffickers (231 for sex trafficking) in the year. A 2024 study it cites found a majority of workers in Nepal's adult entertainment sector were sex-trafficking victims, nearly half of them children. Research collated on Wikipedia gives estimates of 5,000–10,000 Nepali women and girls trafficked to India each year across a 1,850 km open border.
cases.cover_up: US TIP 2025: serious concerns of official complicity; traffickers bribe some Indian officials to fly Nepali workers to third countries.

cases.title: Kamathipura, Mumbai — red-light district fed by trafficking from Nepal and Indian states
cases.who: Brothels of Kamathipura
cases.what: Kamathipura, Mumbai's oldest and largest red-light district and one of Asia's largest, was established over 150 years ago under British rule; the BBC in 2013 put its sex workers at an estimated 20,000. Girls were trafficked there from poor villages in other Indian states, some as young as 11, on promises of domestic work. The 2025 US Trafficking in Persons report is cited, though it could not be opened for this map, for a shift of sex trafficking in India toward spas, hotels and private residences, and for 2022 crime-data figures of 204 convicted traffickers and 1,134 acquittals; that report could not be opened in this pass (state.gov blocked).

flows.title: Canada → Nepal (aid-worker offender)
flows.what: A Canadian humanitarian working with street children abused boys at his home in Nepal.

networks.name: Orphanage trafficking and orphanage tourism (recruitment of children into institutions for donations)
networks.what: A recurring pattern in which orphanages are set up or kept full to attract foreign donations, volunteers and tourists, recruiting children who mostly have living parents, sometimes with payments to families or forged documents. Governments and the US State Department have recognised it as trafficking, and Australia's parliament classed it as modern slavery in 2017.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: Scranton (USA) → Ciudad del Este (Paraguay): Fr Carlos Urrutigoity.
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2008: Paraguay — Comisión de Verdad y Justicia, Informe Final (28 Aug 2008): sexual slavery of girls by senior officers of the Stroessner regime.
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

cases.title: Boystown darknet platform
cases.who: Boystown (Tor platform, about 400,000 registered users)
cases.what: Boystown launched in June 2019, focused on the abuse of boys, and had 400,000 registered users when a BKA-led taskforce with Europol, the Netherlands, Sweden, Australia, Canada and the US took it down in April 2021. Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention. Successor platforms with a common German administrator were shut down around Christmas 2022.

cases.title: Paraguay — Truth and Justice Commission: sexual slavery of girls by senior officers of the Stroessner regime
cases.who: Senior military and police officers of the Stroessner regime; procurers who took girls from their families
cases.what: Paraguay's Comisión de Verdad y Justicia, created by law in October 2003, presented its final report on 28 August 2008 after collecting more than 2,000 testimonies on the 1954–1989 dictatorship. Its conclusions state that sexual violence against women and girls was fostered by the repressive apparatus and reached its extreme in 'sexual slavery of girls practised by senior officers of the regime', and that young children were exploited economically and sexually in military posts at the service of officers. It recorded that 10.8% of victims were minors at the time and noted large under-reporting of sexual violence. Amnesty International reported that girls as young as seven were believed to have been taken from their homes for senior military officers.

cases.title: Paraguay — 47,000 children in criadazgo domestic servitude (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Families taking in children as unpaid domestic workers
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says criadazgo — compelling children to work as domestic workers — is a common form of trafficking in Paraguay; an estimated 47,000 children are in criadazgo, mostly girls (boys are 30 per cent), and many are highly vulnerable to sex and labour trafficking. Colombia's report describes the same practice.

cases.title: Paraguay — Fr Carlos Urrutigoity and the removal of Bishop Livieres
cases.who: Diocese of Ciudad del Este
cases.what: Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity was accused in 2002 in the US of sleeping with boarding-school students, giving them alcohol and sexually abusing a recently graduated seminarian. He then moved to the Diocese of Ciudad del Este, Paraguay, and became its second-in-command in 2014. His case reportedly cost Bishop Livieres his post when Pope Francis removed him in 2014. He was moved back to Mendoza, Argentina, in June 2015. He has not been convicted.
cases.cover_up: After accusations in the US (a 2002 complaint over students at St Gregory's Academy in the Diocese of Scranton), he moved with his group to Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres in 2014; Urrutigoity left in June 2015. La Nación reported at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay.

flows.title: Boystown administrator arrested in Paraguay
flows.what: One of Boystown's German administrators was living in Paraguay and arrested there in April 2021.

flows.title: Scranton (USA) → Ciudad del Este (Paraguay): Fr Carlos Urrutigoity
flows.what: After 2002 accusations in Scranton, the priest and his group moved to Ciudad del Este, where he became vicar general in 2014; he was moved to Mendoza, Argentina in 2015.

networks.name: Roman Catholic Church
networks.what: The Holy See governs about 1.3 billion Catholics. From 1922 (and 1962) canonical abuse cases were handled under strict secrecy; from 2001 they were reserved to the Congregation for the Doctrine of the Faith under pontifical secret, which was lifted in December 2019. National inquiries in Ireland, the US, Australia, Germany, France, the Netherlands, Belgium, Portugal, Spain and elsewhere found bishops moved accused clergy and avoided police. The UN Committee on the Rights of the Child in 2014 found practices that led to impunity.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: Dictatorship or occupation: children given to other families under false identities
patterns.role_note: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–) (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

patterns.pattern: Platforms, servers and the money behind them
patterns.role: Hosts the most reported abuse material (IWF 2025)
patterns.role_note: 6,820 web addresses actioned by the IWF in 2025 (2% of the total).
patterns.pattern_summary: Online abuse of children depends on ordinary businesses: companies that host websites, apps and social platforms, payment services and banks. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that finds and removes abuse images, found most of the material it removed on servers in Bulgaria, the United States, the Netherlands, Romania and France. Reports of suspected abuse to the US CyberTipline, most of them made by American technology companies, rose from 4,560 in 1998 to more than 36 million in 2023, then fell to about 20.5 million in 2024; the centre that runs it attributed part of the fall to Meta encrypting its messages. Money for watching abuse streamed live flows from Australia, Britain, the United States and other wealthy countries to the Philippines. In 2020 the Australian bank Westpac agreed to pay a A$1.3 billion penalty for breaches of money-laundering law that included failing to check payments that could be linked to child exploitation. The classified advertising site Backpage earned more than $500 million from advertisements, including ones used to sell children, before US authorities shut it down in 2018.

cases.title: Project Spade — Azov Films, Toronto
cases.who: Azov Films (Toronto distributor of 'naturist' films of children)
cases.what: Toronto police undercover officers made contact with a man sharing graphic abuse images in October 2010, which led to Azov Films, a Toronto company run by Brian Way that produced and sold films of child exploitation worldwide; after a joint investigation with the US Postal Inspection Service, police raided the business. Police said it was a $4 million business distributing to over 50 countries and seized over 45 terabytes of data. On 14 November 2013 Toronto police announced 348 arrests and 386 children rescued; those arrested included 40 school teachers, nine doctors and nurses, six law enforcement personnel, nine pastors and priests and three foster parents. Way was arrested in 2011 and in 2016 was found guilty of making and distributing child sexual abuse material and sentenced to ten years, reduced after a judge found he had been abused in jail.
cases.cover_up: Germany's BKA received the customer list in October 2011 but began investigating only in October 2012; a German MP on the list later resigned, and information about the case was passed to his party leader.

cases.title: Dreamboard / Operation Delego
cases.who: Dreamboard (invitation-only bulletin board, about 600 members)
cases.what: An invitation-only bulletin board, used by an estimated 600 people, whose applicants had to upload abuse material of children aged 12 or under and keep uploading to stay. NBC reported the computers hosting the site were in Georgia, US, and the top administrators were in France and Canada. In August 2011 Attorney General Eric Holder and DHS Secretary Janet Napolitano announced charges against 72 people, with arrests on five continents including 43 in the US. By January 2013, 57 had been arrested, 45 had pleaded guilty and one was convicted at trial; 42 had been sentenced to between 10 years and life. Fifteen were known only by online identities. DOJ said at least 38 children were being abused by group members.

Three German administrators were arrested in Germany and one German national in Paraguay. In December 2022 they were sentenced to between 7 and 12 years, two with preventive detention.
