cases.title: 764 network — founder sentenced to 80 years
cases.who: 764 (online network on Discord/Telegram; founder Bradley Cadenhead)
cases.what: 764, named after the first digits of the ZIP code of Stephenville, Texas, extorted minors into producing abuse material, self-harm and animal cruelty. Its founder, Bradley Cadenhead, was arrested in August 2021 aged 16 and on 16 May 2023 was sentenced in Texas to 80 years after pleading guilty to nine counts of possession/promotion of child sexual abuse material. The US DOJ describes 764 as a nihilistic violent extremist network and its Counterterrorism Section prosecutes it; on 29 April 2025 DOJ announced the arrests of two alleged leaders of the subgroup '764 Inferno', in North Carolina and in Greece. On 10 December 2025 Canada became the first country to list 764 as a terrorist entity.

cases.title: Wonderland Club / Operation Cathedral
cases.who: The Wonderland Club (encrypted online network)
cases.what: An international online ring that ran for about four years over encrypted internet chat; each new member had to supply 10,000 images of child abuse. Members held at least 750,000 images and 1,800 videos. Led by the UK National Crime Squad, police in 12 to 13 countries (reported figures differ) acted simultaneously on 2 September 1998, about 1,500 officers raiding 107 homes and making 104 arrests. CNN reported in February 2001 that only 17 of the children in the images had been identified, six of them in Britain. The investigation began after US Customs exposed a related ring, the Orchid Club, in 1996.

cases.title: Chile — illegal adoptions abroad, peaking under Pinochet (criminal probe 2018–)
cases.who: Chilean state agencies, hospital and social-service staff, intermediaries
cases.what: Children were taken from mainly poor mothers, some told their babies had died, and sent for adoption to families in the United States and Europe, including Sweden; the practice peaked under the Pinochet dictatorship (1973–1990). A Chilean judge opened a criminal investigation in 2018 covering about 8,000 adoptions abroad from 1970 to 1999. A congressional committee concluded the state was responsible; as of September 2023 nobody had been brought to justice. Sweden opened its own investigation into intercountry adoptions after activism by Chilean adoptees.

cases.title: Guatemala — Peace Archives report: army and state role in adoptions of children during the war (1977–1989)
cases.who: Guatemalan armed forces and National Police; Secretaría de Bienestar Social (Hogar Elisa Martínez); notaries and courts
cases.what: In September 2009 the Dirección de los Archivos de la Paz, part of the Peace Secretariat of the Presidency set up under President Álvaro Colom, published a study of adoptions during the internal armed conflict. It reviewed 333 of 670 adoption files recorded for 1977–1989 and found that the army and National Police transported children into the adoption system, that adoptions often rested on court declarations of abandonment with little effort to find parents, and that a 1977 decree let notaries formalise adoptions without a judge. Chief investigator Marco Tulio Álvarez told the press the children went mainly to the United States, Sweden, Italy and France.
cases.cover_up: Decree 54-77 (1977) let notaries complete adoptions without prior judicial approval; the welfare secretariat kept no record of how many children it received

cases.title: South Korea — Truth and Reconciliation Commission finds state responsible for overseas-adoption abuses
cases.who: South Korean government; private adoption agencies (Wikipedia list cites Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
cases.what: On 26 March 2025, after a two-year inquiry into petitions from 367 adoptees sent abroad between 1964 and 1999 to 11 countries, the commission found human rights violations in at least 56 cases. It found agencies sent set numbers of children each month to meet foreign agencies' demand, falsely registered children with known parents as orphans, did not properly obtain consent and failed to vet adoptive parents. It said the state treated overseas adoption as a cheap alternative to domestic welfare and recommended an official apology and ratification of the Hague Convention. President Lee Jae-myung apologised on 2 October 2025.
cases.cover_up: The commission found the government neglected its duty to oversee agencies; children were falsely registered as orphans and identities were swapped when a child died before departure.

cases.title: Sweden — state inquiry into intercountry adoptions (report 2 June 2025)
cases.who: Swedish state authorities and adoption organisations
cases.what: Sweden's independent inquiry into intercountry adoptions issued its report on 2 June 2025 (nearly 1,600 pages), reviewing 65 years of adoption history and documenting numerous irregularities and illegalities of which state authorities had some knowledge. Sweden had already stopped adoptions from South Korea (AP, 2024). Sweden received 9,051 Korean children 1957–2005, and in January 1975 the Swedish ambassador urged South Korea to continue sending children after it tried to halt adoptions to Scandinavia.

cases.title: Sri Lanka — 1980s 'baby farms' supplying intercountry adoption
cases.who: Baby farms, brokers, hospital doctors and nurses acting as intermediaries for Western agencies
cases.what: A Dutch Zembla documentary (September 2017) reported that babies were bought or abducted from hospitals, handed to paid 'acting mothers' and sold for adoption, mainly to the Netherlands, with others to the UK, Sweden and Germany. Sri Lanka's health minister Rajitha Senaratne acknowledged on camera that 'there were a lot of baby farms back then' and announced an inquiry and a DNA databank. Sri Lanka changed its rules after a 1987 police raid found 20 newborns and 22 women held in 'prison like conditions'.
cases.cover_up: Adoption records were widely falsified; 'acting mothers' were paid to pose as birth mothers in court.

cases.title: Europol: at least 10,000 unaccompanied migrant children missing in Europe (2016)
cases.who: Europol; organized crime exploiting the migrant flow
cases.what: On 31 January 2016 Europol's chief of staff Brian Donald told The Observer that at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, 5,000 of them in Italy and 1,000 in Sweden, and that Europol had evidence some had been sexually exploited. He said an entire criminal infrastructure had developed over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary. Save the Children estimated 26,000 unaccompanied children arrived in 2015.

cases.title: Swedish inquiry into abuse in children's homes and foster care (Vanvårdsutredningen)
cases.who: Swedish municipal children's homes and foster care
cases.what: The government inquiry into abuse and neglect in Swedish children's homes and foster care from 1920 to 1980 reported in February 2011, recommending a public apology and SEK 250,000 for each person who suffered serious abuse; the apology ceremony was held at Stockholm City Hall in 2011. A compensation board set up on 1 January 2013 had decided just over 4,000 applications by July 2015 and rejected 53% of them, with no right of appeal.

cases.title: Operation Atelier — network of abuse photographers
cases.who: Professional photographers producing abuse material
cases.what: Czech-initiated and supported by Europol and Eurojust: a Czech photographer exploited socially and financially disadvantaged children (close to 70) and, with a Swedish partner, distributed images to customers in the EU and Canada. In 2014 ten people were arrested in the Czech Republic (5), Sweden (2), France, Ireland and Spain; 30 TB of data were seized.

cases.title: Kidflix / Operation Stream
cases.who: Kidflix (paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users 2022–2025)
cases.what: Kidflix, created in 2021, let users stream as well as download abuse videos, paying in cryptocurrency converted to tokens; 91,000 unique videos (6,288 hours) were uploaded. German and Dutch authorities seized the server on 11 March 2025, when it held about 72,000 videos. Operation Stream, led by Bavarian police with 38 countries and Europol, identified 1,393 suspects and arrested 79 during action weeks in March 2025; Europol called it the largest child sexual exploitation operation in its history.

cases.title: Norway-led crypto-tracing operation: 28 arrests (2026)
cases.who: Buyers paying cryptocurrency for dark web forum access
cases.what: From late May to mid-June 2026 police in Canada, Czechia, Germany, Norway, Poland, Sweden and Switzerland arrested 28 men aged 22–54 suspected of paying cryptocurrency to access dark web forums with abuse videos; one used AI to generate material and some victims were family members. Norwegian police used a crypto-tracing method developed in 2025, which also identified two sellers.

cases.title: Operation Cumberland — AI-generated abuse material platform
cases.who: Paid platform distributing AI-generated abuse material (Danish main suspect)
cases.what: A Danish national arrested in November 2024 ran a platform distributing AI-generated abuse material he produced; users paid a symbolic fee for a password. Most arrests came on 26 February 2025 in an operation led by Danish police with 18 other countries; 273 suspects were identified and 25 arrested. Europol called it one of the first cases involving AI-generated CSAM and noted the lack of national laws covering it.

flows.title: Seoul → Sweden
flows.what: South Korean children sent for adoption to Sweden; part of about 163,898 sent abroad 1953–2008. The 2025 Truth and Reconciliation Commission found state-enabled fraud in overseas adoptions.

flows.title: Colombo → Sweden
flows.what: Sri Lankan children adopted to Sweden in the 1980s (baby-farm period).

flows.title: Santiago → Sweden
flows.what: Children taken from Chilean mothers and adopted in Sweden, peaking under Pinochet; Sweden opened its own inquiry.

flows.title: Athens → Sweden
flows.what: Greek-born children adopted to Sweden 1950–1975; Greece restored their citizenship by law on 2 May 2025.

networks.name: South Korea's four authorised overseas adoption agencies (Holt Children's Services, Eastern Social Welfare Society, Korea Social Service, Korea Welfare Services)
networks.what: The four agencies held guardianship over children and sent them abroad under government policy; Holt sent about half (AP). The TRC (March 2025) found agencies met monthly quotas for foreign partners, falsified orphan status and swapped identities, and that the state failed to supervise them. All four were implicated in the petitions (Guardian, 2023).

networks.name: Dreamboard
networks.what: Invitation-only board, about 600 members; 72 charged in Operation Delego (2011). Start year is approximate (investigation launched 2009).

networks.name: Boystown
networks.what: Tor platform with 400,000 registered users; four German administrators sentenced 7–12 years (2022).

networks.name: Kidflix
networks.what: Paid streaming platform, 1.8 million users (2022–2025), 91,000 videos; 1,393 suspects identified, 79 arrested.
Online network extorting minors into producing abuse material and self-harm; fragmented into subgroups (CVLT, 676, etc.) within 'The Com'.

networks.name: Livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines (OSEC)
networks.what: Not one organisation: thousands of local traffickers, often parents or relatives, paid by foreign buyers to livestream abuse. IJM: 1 in 100 Filipino children affected in 2022.

patterns.pattern: Waves of reckoning, and the countries that never looked
patterns.role_note: 2016: Turkey — Grand National Assembly research commission on preventing child abuse (set up 24 March 2016 after the Ensar Foundation dormitory case in Karaman; report Oct–Nov 2016).
patterns.pattern_summary: Governments and churches held official inquiries into child abuse in institutions at different times. Canada's Hughes inquiry into the Mount Cashel orphanage began in 1989, and Ireland's Commission to Inquire into Child Abuse ran from 1999 to 2009. In the United States, Catholic bishops commissioned a national study that was published in 2004, and state grand juries and attorneys general followed. Germany, Belgium, the Netherlands and Austria began inquiries after a wave of disclosures in 2010. Australia's Royal Commission sat from 2013 to 2017, the inquiry for England and Wales ran from 2014 to 2022, and New Zealand's from 2018 to 2024. France, Portugal, Spain and Switzerland reported between 2021 and 2023. Several of these studies were commissioned and paid for by the Catholic Church itself. Where an inquiry surveyed the general population instead of relying on church records, the numbers were much higher: France's commission estimated that about 216,000 people had been abused as children by priests and members of religious orders since 1950, compared with about 3,000 cases the church had identified. In Italy the only national figures come from reports the Italian bishops' conference has published about itself since 2022. Brazil's Congress held inquiries into the sexual exploitation of children that reported in 2004, 2010 and 2014. The research for this map found no national inquiry into abuse in institutions in the Philippines or India; India's official findings are state-level audits of children's homes, such as the 2018 audit of 110 homes in Bihar.

patterns.pattern: Officials who took part or looked away
patterns.role_note: Jordan and Türkiye — Syrian refugee girls in forced marriages and sex trafficking (US TIP 2025).
patterns.pattern_summary: In 282 cases on this map, police officers, prosecutors, judges, politicians, civil servants, soldiers or intelligence officers took part in the abuse, or a court or inquiry found that they ignored, concealed or obstructed it. In Rotherham, in the north of England, an independent inquiry in 2014 estimated that about 1,400 children had been sexually exploited between 1997 and 2013 and called the failures of the council and the police "blatant"; three earlier reports had been suppressed or ignored. In Australia in 1972, a senior police officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. In North Wales, the police investigated allegations against their own officers. In Mexico, after the journalist Lydia Cacho exposed an abuse ring in Cancún, Puebla state police arrested her in 2005, and leaked phone calls recorded the state governor discussing her detention; he was arrested in 2021 on torture charges.

cases.title: Turkey — parliamentary research commission on child abuse after the Ensar Foundation dormitory case (2016)
cases.who: Student houses in Karaman linked to the Ensar Foundation; student dormitories nationally
cases.what: On 24 March 2016 the Turkish Grand National Assembly unanimously set up a research commission on child abuse after a teacher in Karaman was arrested for abusing 10 children in student houses, two of them owned by the Ensar Foundation. It began work on 28 April; by July its only field visit had been to Karaman, where the provincial family directorate gave members a report that blamed the victims' families. Its draft report in October 2016 recommended that the Education Ministry license and inspect student dormitories, a permanent children's rights committee in parliament, a child-protection coordination centre, background checks for people working with children and a wider penal definition of sexual abuse. Opposition (CHP) members said the report was general and theoretical and that the commission had not visited state nurseries, prisons or Syrian camps.

cases.title: ISIS genocide of Yazidis — abduction, sale and sexual slavery of women and girls
cases.who: Islamic State (ISIS/Da'esh)
cases.what: ISIS attacked Sinjar on 3 August 2014 and moved captured Yazidis in an organised manner to holding sites in Tal Afar, Mosul (Badoush prison, the Galaxy wedding hall) and Baaj, and women and girls onward to Raqqa in Syria. The UN Commission of Inquiry on Syria found in June 2016 ('They came to destroy') that ISIS committed genocide; women and girls, some as young as nine, were sold at market and held in sexual slavery, and boys were forced into ISIS training camps. At that date over 3,200 Yazidi women and children were still held, mostly in Syria; thousands remain missing.

cases.title: 'Sweetie' sting — 20,000 offers to pay for webcam abuse
cases.who: Terre des hommes Netherlands (virtual 10-year-old 'Sweetie')
cases.what: In a 10-week investigation run from a warehouse in Amsterdam, Terre des hommes Netherlands posed in public chatrooms as 'Sweetie', a computer-generated 10-year-old Filipina girl, to show the scale of webcam child sex abuse: 20,000 internet users offered to pay for webcam sex performances. The researchers identified about 1,000 of them, from 65 countries, including 110 in the UK and 254 traced to computers in the US, and on 4 November 2013 handed their details to Interpol. They said online child exploitation had become a hardened criminal industry in the Philippines.

cases.title: Jordan and Türkiye — Syrian refugee girls in forced marriages and sex trafficking (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Families and brokers arranging unofficial marriages
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says Syrian girls in Türkiye — which hosted about 2.9 million displaced Syrians — are forced into marriages in unofficial religious ceremonies, particularly in poor rural regions, and then subjected to domestic servitude and sex trafficking. In Jordan, Syrian refugee women and girls have been sold into forced marriages, and in 2022 authorities investigated a mother for allegedly exploiting her two daughters with foreign tourists.
cases.cover_up: Türkiye: no investigations of complicit officials reported, though corruption and complicity remained significant concerns.

cases.title: Ankara prosecutors' inquiry into alleged trafficking of girls from Turkey to Epstein
cases.who: Ankara Chief Public Prosecutor's Office (inquiry)
cases.what: On 23 Dec 2025 Ankara prosecutors reportedly opened an inquiry after opposition MP Turhan Çömez cited the DOJ files. The underlying document is a May 2009 civil complaint by 'Jane Doe No. 102' alleging 'upon information and belief' that Epstein brought minor girls from 'Turkey, the Czech Republic, Asia, and numerous other countries'. Prosecutors are reviewing the files; no findings or charges have been reported.

flows.title: Moldova → Russia, Turkey, Israel, UAE (trafficking of women and children, incl. institution leavers)
flows.what: The US State Department (March 2007) reported women and children trafficked from Moldova for sexual exploitation, increasingly to Russia and the Middle East including Turkey, Israel and the UAE; UNICEF found children leaving Moldova's residential institutions were several times more vulnerable to trafficking than other children.

networks.name: Islamic State (ISIS / Da'esh)
networks.what: ISIS abducted thousands of Yazidi women and children from Sinjar in August 2014 and ran markets for their sale; the UN COI found genocide. Affiliates in West Africa, the Sahel and Mozambique are verified by the UN as abducting children.

networks.name: Jeffrey Epstein and associates
networks.what: Financier Jeffrey Epstein (d. 2019) and Ghislaine Maxwell (convicted 2021) sexually abused and trafficked girls, some as young as 14, between at least 1994 and 2005 across homes in New York, Palm Beach, New Mexico, the US Virgin Islands, Paris and London. Model agent Jean-Luc Brunel was charged in France and died in custody. Banks paid hundreds of millions in settlements. 2025–2026 file releases led to misconduct and corruption inquiries against officials in the UK and Norway.

patterns.pattern: Moved instead of stopped
patterns.role_note: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa').
patterns.pattern_summary: When a priest, religious brother, teacher or head teacher was found to be abusing children, the institution they worked for often moved them instead of reporting them to the police. The move was to another parish, another school, another state or another country, and the person went on working with children. A Pennsylvania grand jury reported in 2018 that bishops in six dioceses had moved priests they knew to be abusers. In Australia, Bishop Mulkearns knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept appointing him to new parishes. In Melbourne in 2008, the Adass Israel School paid for its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to fly to Israel before the police were told of the allegations against her. In England, an internal report in 1982 described how the barrister John Smyth had beaten boys he met through evangelical holiday camps; he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, the police were not told until 2013, and a 2024 review called him "a problem solved and exported to Africa". The map draws 34 documented moves and colors the countries that sent or received an abuser.

patterns.pattern: Children taken by governments, then abused or given false identities
patterns.role: State schools and programmes where removed children were sexually abused
patterns.role_note: British child migration programmes — IICSA (receiving or involved).
patterns.pattern_summary: In several countries the government itself took children from their parents, and the records show those children were then sexually abused or handed to other families under false identities. During Argentina's military dictatorship from 1976 to 1983, babies born to women held in secret detention were taken and given to military families and allies of the regime. In 2012 a Buenos Aires court found this had been a "systematic plan" and sentenced the former dictator Jorge Videla to 50 years. By July 2025 the Grandmothers of Plaza de Mayo had identified 140 of those children. Uruguay, Chile, El Salvador and Franco's Spain had similar cases, in which children were taken without their parents' consent and adopted by other families at home or abroad, often under changed names. Nazi Germany took children from occupied Poland and placed them with German families under new identities. In Canada and the United States, Indigenous children were sent to government-funded residential and boarding schools. Canada's Truth and Reconciliation Commission reported in 2015, and by the end of 2014 nearly 38,000 claims had been made for physical and sexual abuse at the schools. A US federal report in 2022 said many children at its 417 boarding schools suffered physical, sexual and emotional abuse. Britain sent children abroad to Australia, Canada and other countries under child migration schemes, and a 2018 inquiry found evidence that children sent under these schemes were sexually abused. In Ireland and South Korea, inquiries found that adoption agencies working with the state falsely registered children as orphans or hid their identities.

cases.title: British child migration programmes — IICSA
cases.who: UK government; Fairbridge Society, Barnardo's, Sisters of Nazareth, Catholic Church agencies and others; receiving institutions incl. Christian Brothers
cases.what: IICSA's report of 1 March 2018 found that the child migration programmes were 'a deeply flawed government policy' and that successive UK governments failed to ensure protections against abuse. It found a catalogue of evidence that migrated children suffered ill-treatment and abuse including sexual abuse; Barnardo's suspended migration after sexual abuse came to light at its Picton school, and the Fairbridge Society failed to respond to allegations at its schools in Canada and Australia. It recommended an immediate financial redress scheme for surviving child migrants.
cases.cover_up: Successive governments continued the policy despite years of evidence that children were suffering, including sexual abuse. Fairbridge failed to respond properly to a series of sexual abuse allegations at its schools.

cases.title: Zimbabwe — Gender Commission inquiry into sexual exploitation of girls and child marriage in apostolic sects (2021–2023)
cases.who: Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect and other apostolic church branches
cases.what: After a 14-year-old girl died in childbirth at a Johanne Marange Apostolic Sect shrine in August 2021, the Zimbabwe Gender Commission opened a public investigation on 24 September 2021 into sexual exploitation and abuse of girls and child marriages in apostolic sects. It identified compulsory virginity testing, wife pledging, betrothal and forced marriage in the Marange sect, and an earlier 2020 probe of branches around Marondera found girls of about 10 to 15 taken in as 'wives-in-waiting' and married at puberty. Its report for 2022 said it had received and investigated over 500 cases of child marriage and sexual exploitation and called for legislation regulating faith-based organisations.

cases.title: John Smyth — Iwerne camps, Zimbabwe and South Africa (Makin Review)
cases.who: Iwerne Trust (evangelical camps), Church of England; Zambesi Ministries (Zimbabwe); Anglican Church of Southern Africa
cases.what: John Smyth QC, chair of the Iwerne Trust 1974–81, beat and abused boys and young men he met through the evangelical Iwerne camps and Winchester College's Christian Forum. After the 1982 Ruston Report he moved to Zimbabwe in 1984, founding Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986; a 16-year-old died at one of his camps in December 1992 and Smyth was arrested in 1997 but never charged anywhere. Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, he moved to South Africa in 2001 and the review found abuse likely continued until his death in Cape Town on 11 August 2018. Keith Makin's review was published on 7 November 2024; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.
cases.cover_up: A 1982 internal Iwerne Trust report (the Ruston Report) described the beatings; the Makin Review found an 'active cover-up' by its recipients; police were not told until 2013. The review called Smyth 'a problem solved and exported to Africa' and found no evidence of proactive attempts to alert Zimbabwean authorities.

cases.title: Zimbabwe — sex trafficking around gold and diamond mines; girls traded under ngozi (US TIP 2025)
cases.who: Traffickers at mining sites; families
cases.what: The 2025 US TIP report says traffickers exploit women and children in sex trafficking around mines, sometimes for money or food, and may exploit children as panners and ore couriers in gold and diamond mines. Traditional practices including trading daughters for food or money and ngozi — giving a relative to another family to atone for a killing — make girls vulnerable. Low-level official complicity persisted.

flows.title: UK → Southern Rhodesia child migrants (Rhodesia Fairbridge Memorial College)
flows.what: IICSA found that children who told the headmaster they had been sexually abused by a padre at the college were beaten and warned against 'spreading malicious lies'; it lacked evidence to say whether Fairbridge UK knew of the allegations.

flows.title: England → Zimbabwe (John Smyth 'exported to Africa')
flows.what: After the 1982 Ruston Report on his beatings was kept from police, Smyth moved to Zimbabwe in 1984 and founded Zambesi Ministries camps for boys in 1986. The Makin Review called him 'a problem solved and exported to Africa'.

flows.title: Zimbabwe → South Africa (John Smyth)
flows.what: Refused re-entry to Zimbabwe, Smyth moved to South Africa in 2001, attending churches in Durban (from 2002) and Cape Town (Church on Main, 2004–2016). The Makin Review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in 2018.

networks.name: British child migration programmes
networks.what: UK government-backed schemes run by Barnardo's, the Fairbridge Society, Catholic agencies and others that sent children to Canada, Australia, New Zealand and Southern Rhodesia; IICSA found sexual abuse and failure to protect.

networks.name: Church of England
networks.what: IICSA counted 390 convicted offenders associated with the Church of England from the 1940s to 2018 and found a culture of deference and secrecy. The Peter Ball case and the Makin Review of John Smyth showed senior clergy withholding evidence; Archbishop Justin Welby resigned on 12 November 2024.

networks.name: Anglican Communion (national Anglican churches)
networks.what: National Anglican churches with documented findings: Australia (1,082 complainants 1980–2015), Canada (residential schools; Nakayama), New Zealand (Dilworth School), and southern Africa (Smyth).
